quoted_clause: This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand

correction: Replace with: aggregate goodput = number of independent replicas × per-replica goodput; within a TP/PP replica, devices do not multiply token rate. Add a worked check using the 70B TP=8 host.
acceptance_test: Revise §4 item 3 and verify no example computes 8 × 19,780 for the 70B TP=8 host; the 8×H100 host must remain ~19,800 prefill tokens/s.

fix_instruction: Restate item 3: per-replica goodput x independent replicas; TP/PP devices do not multiply token rate.

observed: The '~10× per host-equivalent' comparison is ambiguous. If it means one 7B card (24,725 tok/s) vs one 70B card running the full model unsharded (2,472 tok/s), the ratio is 10×, but calling a single GPU a 'host-equivalent' is incorrect — a host has 8 GPUs. If it means a full host of 7B cards (8 × 24,725 = 197,800) vs one 70B host under TP=8 (19,800), the ratio is also 10×, but this compares 8 independent 7B instances to 1 sharded 70B instance — a different architecture. The text does not explain which comparison is intended.
correction: Replace with an explicit comparison, e.g. '~10× if a full host runs 8 independent 7B instances (197,800 tok/s) vs one 70B host under TP=8 (19,800 tok/s)' or '~10× vs the 70B's full-model-equivalent single-card rate (2,472 tok/s)'.

fix_instruction: Relabel 19,780 as the TP=8 host aggregate and state the pair: 24,725/2,472 ~10x per GPU; 197,800/19,780 ~10x per host.

quoted_clause: Memory fit: 140 GB weights + 24 GB KV = 164 GB < 640 GB aggregate
observed: The 164 GB check is a single-request residency check, not the workload memory gate. At the canonical 10 rps average and 8.6 s service time, Little's Law gives ~86 in-flight requests; 86 × 24 GB ≈ 2,064 GB KV for Candidate (a), and 86 × 1.2 GB ≈ 103 GB KV for Candidate (c). A single 640 GB host or 80 GB H100 therefore does not hold the workload's KV population. At 40 rps peak, ~344 in-flight requests imply ~8.3 TB and ~413 GB respectively.
correction: Define the memory gate at workload concurrency, or explicitly separate 'single-request residency' from 'workload KV residency'. State that Candidate (a) as a one-host deployment fails workload KV residency at average and peak; Candidate (c) as a one-card deployment also fails at average concurrency. Recompute host/card counts from KV capacity, not only prefill throughput.
acceptance_test: Recompute 10 × 8.6 × 24 = 2,064 GB and 40 × 8.6 × 24 = 8,256 GB for (a); 10 × 8.6 × 1.2 = 103.2 GB and 40 × 8.6 × 1.2 = 412.8 GB for (c). Update Candidate (a)/(c) verdicts, Table 12-1 '✓ memory' cells, and mini-case 'fits the memory budget' statements so no single host/card is called memory-feasible for the workload.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md:19 single-request 164 GB 'memory gate passes with one host', Table 12-1 (:89) 'memory 164 < 640'; workload KV 86x24.1 ~2,073 GB; chapter's own ~6-host KV screen contradicts one-host pass.
fix_instruction: Split the gate into single-request residency vs workload KV residency; mark (a) check residency/x workload (~6 hosts), (c) ~2 cards at average; fix Table 12-1 cells.

page_hint: Ch 12, §1 'Concept', para. 4 (page not determinable from chunk)
quoted_clause: Any architecture that violates any one of these is eliminated before evaluation — candidates that fail a gate are not finalists (a *finalist* is a candidate advanced to evaluation; a *conditional finalist* is one advanced with its gate still open): they return to synthesis or are carried forward only as labeled sensitivity cases.

(a) 'eliminated before evaluation' cannot apply to the quality gate, since quality is only knowable by evaluation — and the same paragraph says 'a smaller-model candidate whose quality is unmeasured is gated, not promoted'. quoted_clause: Tokens-per-second that a single device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware. This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand (92K input tokens/s average, 3K output tokens/s average, 368K input tokens/s peak, 12K output tokens/s peak).
observed: §4 instructs the reader to multiply a single device's token rate by the number of devices in the layout. §3 of the same chapter spends four sentences correcting exactly this error for the canonical layout: under TP=8 the host aggregate equals the per-GPU rate (~19,800 tok/s), not 8x it, because each GPU carries 1/8 of the FLOPs for the same shared token stream. The chapter therefore states the rule and its negation within ~1,500 words, and the §4 statement is the wrong one.
correction: Rewrite §4 item 3 to state the rule with its scope: 'A device rate may be multiplied by the number of devices only when those devices are independent replicas (data parallel). Inside a tensor-parallel group every device advances the same token stream with a fraction of the FLOPs, so the group's aggregate rate equals the per-device rate, not N times it. The screen is therefore: per-replica rate x number of replicas.' Add a one-line worked cross-check (17.5 GFLOP/token/GPU -> 19,780 tok/s -> host aggregate 19,780) so the rule and §3 cannot drift apart again.
acceptance_test: A reader who applies §4's rule to the canonical 8xH100 layout obtains 19,780 tok/s (not 158,240) and reproduces the ~5-host average prefill screen and the ~21-host peak KV screen. No sentence in Ch 12 or Ch 13 multiplies a per-device rate by a tensor-parallel group size.
verdict_evidence: ch12:45 'multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout' contradicts ch12:19: TP=8 host aggregate = per-GPU 19,780 tok/s 'not 8x a per-GPU rate'; x8=158,240 = 8x host ceiling.
fix_instruction: Rewrite section 4 item 3: multiply per-replica rate by replicas only; TP group aggregate equals per-device rate. Add the 19,780 cross-check.

quoted_clause: the architect's first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget, shape peak demand, or revisit the model class. ... Its memory and economics are trivially favorable; its fate turns on that measured gate. Because candidate (c)'s quality gate is still open **[HYPOTHESIS]**, it is not a finalist — and it stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather than being excluded pre-measurement; the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b), and the near-term decision falls between them.

Yet the mini-case then excludes (c) from the finalist set on the strength of an open quality gate, asserts that (c)'s economics are 'trivially favorable' without a number, and declares that the decision falls between (a) and (b) — two candidates whose own economics fail the budget by 10.4x and 15.5x. The chapter's conclusion therefore excludes the only candidate that could plausibly satisfy the binding constraint, on a gate that is not the binding constraint.

If (c) is still excluded, the chapter must say why the budget cannot be met by any candidate and what the architect presents to the stakeholder.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (b); §3 'Memory/residency arithmetic summary'; Table 12-1 (b) memory cell; §8
quoted_clause: Each pool therefore needs its own 8×H100 host (residency = 140 GB weights plus the pool's in-flight KV population — at the canonical per-host KV budget (640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17), 140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom; co-residency beyond the canonical KV budget requires reducing the KV allocation or adding memory; one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population).
observed: The same 436 GB KV population is applied to both pools, and 'zero headroom' is asserted for both. That is true only for the decode pool, which must hold the KV of every in-flight decode. The prefill pool holds KV only transiently for requests currently being prefilled (and hands it off), so its KV population is far smaller and it has substantial headroom. The chapter's own parenthetical ('one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population') shows the author is aware that pool populations differ, but the arithmetic then treats them as identical.
correction: Split the statement: the decode pool's requirement is 140 GB weights + up to 436 GB of resident decode KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB (zero headroom at the canonical budget); the prefill pool's requirement is 140 GB weights + a transient KV working set (bounded by the number of concurrent prefills, not by the decode population) + ~64 GB runtime, leaving the balance of the 436 GB as headroom. Update Table 12-1's (b) memory cell and the §3 summary accordingly.
acceptance_test: Table 12-1's (b) memory cell distinguishes the two pools' KV populations, and the 'zero headroom' claim is attached to the decode pool only.
verdict_evidence: ch12:22,27 apply 140+436+64=640 GB 'zero headroom' to both pools; prefill KV transient (40 rps x ~1.1 s ~44 reqs ~1.1 TB over ~19 hosts) so 436 GB is decode-pool requirement.
fix_instruction: Split it: zero headroom for the decode pool, transient KV working set for prefill; update Table 12-1's (b) memory cell.

fix_instruction: Drop '~10x per host-equivalent', or label it as an 8-card node comparison beside (c)'s 1.25x per card.

quoted_clause: The 4-bit KV cache is a *memory* optimization, not a quality one; aggressive KV quantization can add its own quality penalty that must also be validated on the target workload.
observed: The two clauses joined by the semicolon contradict each other. 'Not a quality one' read literally means the change has no quality effect, which the second clause denies. The intended meaning is that the change is introduced for memory reasons and is not expected to improve quality — but as written the sentence licenses the inference that 4-bit KV is quality-neutral, which is exactly the inference the chapter's own §7 open question and §5 common mistake ('Using KV-quantization as a free lunch') exist to prevent.
correction: Rewrite: 'The 4-bit KV cache is introduced as a *memory* optimization, not as a quality improvement; it can nonetheless add its own quality penalty, which must be validated on the target workload.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in the book asserts or implies that KV quantization is quality-neutral; a reader who reads §3's sentence cannot conclude that 4-bit KV is free.
verdict_evidence: ch12:25 'a memory optimization, not a quality one; aggressive KV quantization can add its own quality penalty' — self-contradictory; section 5 (53) and 7 (68) assert KV-quant quality loss.
fix_instruction: Rewrite: 'introduced as a memory optimization, not a quality improvement; it can nonetheless add a quality penalty to validate.'
